# Rediscovered: The Untold Innocence of Marilyn Monroe

*(CNN)* — These photographs predate the moment Marilyn Monroe became indelibly branded as the voluptuous blonde bombshell who radiated sex appeal across dozens of Hollywood films. A 24-year-old Monroe poses for *Life* magazine in August 1950—captured before whispers of an affair with President John F. Kennedy began to circulate, before her private struggles with mental health became public knowledge, and long before the mysterious overdose that would claim her life at the age of 36.

Within a collection unearthed by Life.com last month, these previously unpublished photographs reveal a gentler, more unguarded 24-year-old starlet—a young woman on the cusp of stardom, captured during a quieter chapter before fame fully claimed her. Her face, remarkably natural and largely free of makeup, offers a striking departure from the glamorized image of lipstick, designer gowns, and lavish jewelry so often associated with her public persona. Monday would have marked Monroe's 83rd birthday.

In one image, a young Monroe reclines contentedly on a park bench, absorbed in a book—a scene editors at Life.com believe was captured at Griffith Park in Los Angeles. In another, she stands barefoot on a bridge, her expression calm and unguarded. The session, dating to 1950, was the work of *Life* photographer Ed Clark, and it offers a rare glimpse of Monroe that the public has seldom encountered.

"She hadn't yet exploded as a star, but she was clearly on the brink of something big," said Dawnie Walton, deputy editor at Life.com, a site housing more than 7 million *Life* magazine photographs and launched this past March. "I was struck by her face. There's an innocence to it, yet also something undeniably alluring."

Walton discovered the rare images last month while sifting through the company's digital photo archives—photographs that, it seems, no one at Life.com even knew existed. Upon closer investigation, she found scant documentation accompanying the negatives, leading her to believe they were likely intended for a cover shoot that was ultimately never used. Monroe would not grace her first *Life* cover until 1952. 

*See some of the previously unpublished photos of Monroe »*

"It simply got lost, tucked away," Walton explained. "It had been sitting in a warehouse somewhere in New Jersey."

At the time these photographs were taken, Monroe had just landed her first notable film role, playing a mistress in *The Asphalt Jungle*. She was still primarily known as a model, having appeared only in a handful of film cameos. Photographer Ed Clark later recounted to the *Sarasota Herald-Tribune* how a friend at 20th Century Fox had tipped him off that the studio had just signed "a hot tomato."

"She was unknown then, so I was able to spend a great deal of time photographing her," Clark recalled. "We'd go out to Griffith Park, and she would read poetry. I sent several rolls of film to *Life* in New York, but they wired back, 'Who the hell is Marilyn Monroe?'"

The images that would follow later in the 1950s and into the early 1960s portrayed a far more confident and overtly sensual Monroe—photographs destined to become icons of popular culture. Among them is the now-legendary image of Monroe in a white halter dress, her skirt billowing upward, taken in 1955 to promote *The Seven Year Itch*. In 1962, photographer Bert Stern captured a series of intimate, sometimes nude images of Monroe in what would become known as "The Last Sitting." She died roughly six weeks later, on August 5, 1962.

According to Life.com staff, the *Life* archive contains some 15 million photographs dating back to the late 1850s—predating the magazine's official launch in 1936. Two years ago, the publication began the gradual process of digitizing this vast collection. Occasionally, previously unknown photographs surface unexpectedly; in other cases, images were taken but simply never selected for publication.

Last March, to mark the 11th anniversary of Frank Sinatra's death, Life.com released a series of unpublished photographs of the singer. Then in April, the site unveiled newly recovered, never-before-seen images of Martin Luther King Jr., taken by a *Life* photographer on the day of King's assassination at a Memphis, Tennessee, hotel in 1968.

Long before she became the platinum-haired icon draped in white silk over a subway grate, before the whispered scandals, the tumultuous marriages, and the tragic end that would forever complicate her legacy, there was simply Norma Jeane—a 24-year-old actress named Marilyn Monroe, still finding her footing in Hollywood. A newly rediscovered trove of photographs, taken in 1950 by acclaimed Life photographer Ed Clark, offers an extraordinary window into this fleeting, unguarded moment in her life, just before the world would come to know her as one of the most photographed women of the 20th century.

The images, unearthed by editors at Life.com while combing through the magazine's vast archives, had never been published. They sat forgotten for decades, quiet relics of a photo shoot that captured something far more intimate than the polished, hyper-glamorous persona Monroe would later cultivate for the cameras. In these shots, there is no heavy makeup, no calculated poses, no trace of the bombshell image that would soon define her career and, in many ways, consume her identity.

Instead, we see a young woman at ease. In one series of photographs, Monroe relaxes in a park, her expression soft and unguarded, seemingly unaware—or unconcerned—with how she might be perceived. In another, she stands barefoot on a bridge, her hair falling naturally, her feet bare against the wood, looking less like an emerging sex symbol and more like any young woman enjoying a quiet afternoon outdoors. There's a playfulness to some frames, a pensiveness to others, but throughout, an unmistakable authenticity that stands in stark contrast to the meticulously constructed Marilyn Monroe the public would soon come to idolize.

What makes these photographs so poignant is their timing. In 1950, Monroe was still on the cusp of the fame that would transform her life irrevocably. She had appeared in small film roles and was beginning to attract attention, but the full weight of stardom—with all its glittering rewards and devastating costs—had not yet arrived. The image she would become known for, the breathy voice and sultry glamour, was still being shaped, both by studio executives and by Monroe herself.

Looking at these images now, decades later, it's impossible not to feel the weight of hindsight. We know what lies ahead for this young woman: the meteoric rise to becoming one of the most famous actresses in the world, the tumultuous relationships with Joe DiMaggio and Arthur Miller, the growing dependence on prescription medications, the public unraveling, and ultimately, her death in 1962 at just 36 years old—a loss that would cement her as a tragic symbol of Hollywood's often merciless machinery.

But in Ed Clark's photographs, none of that has happened yet. There is only a young woman, barefoot on a bridge or lounging in dappled sunlight, her future still unwritten. These images offer viewers something rare: a chance to see Marilyn Monroe not as a legend, not as a cultural icon weighted down by decades of mythology, but simply as herself—unpolished, unguarded, and entirely human. It's a reminder that before she became "Marilyn Monroe" in the fullest, most complicated sense of that name, she was simply a young woman named Norma Jeane, standing at the threshold of a fame she could not yet fully comprehend.

*A previously unseen collection of images resurfaces, joining a growing archive of rediscovered celebrity photography*

A trove of long-forgotten photographs of Marilyn Monroe has been uncovered, giving fans and historians a fresh look at the Hollywood icon during the later, more complex chapters of her career. The images, found in archival storage after decades of obscurity, capture Monroe away from the glossy studio portraits that made her one of the most photographed women of the 20th century.

## A Star in Transition

By the early 1960s, Monroe was working to redefine herself as a serious actress, moving beyond the "blonde bombshell" persona that had made her famous in films like *Gentlemen Prefer Blondes* and *How to Marry a Millionaire*. She had studied at the Actors Studio in New York, married and divorced playwright Arthur Miller, and was pushing for more dramatic roles that showcased range beyond comedic performances.

The newly surfaced photographs reportedly show Monroe during this period of reinvention—candid, contemplative, and markedly different from the polished glamour shots that made her an enduring symbol of Hollywood's Golden Age. That iconic imagery, including the swirling white dress from *The Seven Year Itch* and countless studio portraits emphasizing her platinum hair and magnetic gaze, cemented her status as one of the most recognizable faces in entertainment history.

Monroe's life was cut short on August 5, 1962, when she was found dead at her Los Angeles home at age 36. Her death, officially ruled a probable suicide from barbiturate overdose, remains a subject of fascination and speculation six decades later, having spawned countless documentaries, books, and conspiracy theories.

## Part of a Larger Pattern of Rediscovery

This find is far from an isolated case. In recent years, archives—particularly those tied to *Life* magazine's massive photographic legacy—have yielded remarkable troves of unseen images depicting other 20th-century icons.

Photographs of Frank Sinatra, capturing the singer both on stage and in unguarded private moments, emerged from *Life.com*'s archives, revealing dimensions of "Ol' Blue Eyes" that had never reached the public. Similarly, previously unpublished images of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. surfaced, offering intimate perspectives on the civil rights leader during pivotal moments of the movement—images that added nuance to the historical record of his activism and personal life.

These archival discoveries underscore how the golden era of magazine photojournalism—when publications like *Life* employed armies of photographers documenting every angle of American culture—left behind vast, still-unexplored repositories of film negatives and prints. Many were shot for stories that were never published, or images that editors passed over in favor of other selections, leaving thousands of frames essentially frozen in time.

## Why These Discoveries Matter

For historians and pop culture enthusiasts alike, each new discovery offers a chance to reexamine familiar figures through an unfiltered lens. Unlike the carefully curated images approved for magazine covers or promotional materials, these forgotten photographs often capture subjects in transitional, vulnerable, or simply mundane moments—humanizing figures who have since ascended to near-mythological status.

As archival technology improves and institutions continue digitizing decades-old negatives, experts suggest more such discoveries are likely on the horizon, each one adding fresh texture to the visual history of some of the most scrutinized figures of the last century.

By 1950, Marilyn Monroe was still very much an emerging starlet, not yet the household name she'd become.
